sentences.text: Qantassaurus was a small, two-legged plant-eater about the size of a grey kangaroo, standing one meter high and measuring 1.8 meters in length.

Its feet had claws for traction, and a long tail stiffened by ossified tendons likely helped it turn quickly. The mouth featured a beak and ten leaf-shaped cheek teeth in each lower jaw that were shed and replaced as they wore down.
Large eye sockets suggest it could see well during long periods of darkness.
Despite its small size, the dinosaur possessed large eye sockets adapted for seeing in the dark.
A long tail stiffened by ossified tendons likely aided in rapid turning.

The genus was described by Rich and Vickers-Rich in 1999 based on a holotype found on February 27, 1996, during the third annual field season of the Dinosaur Dreaming project. Nicole Evered, a long-time participant in the excavation, discovered the specimen on the beach of Bunurong Marine Park at Flat Rocks near Inverloch in southeastern Victoria.
The name honors the Australian airline Qantas.
There are currently two fossil occurrences recorded for this species.
This browser likely grabbed ferns and other vegetation with its five-fingered hands before fleeing from predators like a modern gazelle.
Researchers suggest it was a fast runner capable of escaping danger.
The bone structure suggests it was warm-blooded, a trait that would help maintain body heat in cold environments.
Evidence from related taxa indicates it was active year-round and did not hibernate during winter.
Conditions were likely coldest during polar nights that lasted up to three months.
It may have possessed some form of defensive camouflage, such as spots or stripes.
Qantassaurus is a basal, two-legged, plant-eating ornithischian dinosaur belonging to the clade Elasmaria and the class Ornithischia.

It was originally assigned to Hypsilophodontidae in 1999, but this group is now understood to be an unnatural, paraphyletic group. Recent analysis by Boyd in 2015 recovered it as a basal iguanodontian.

The dinosaur lived in Australia approximately 125 to 112 million years ago, during the Late Aptian or Early Albian of the Early Cretaceous period. At that time, Australia was part of the supercontinent Gondwana and lay partly within the Antarctic Circle.
Some sources list the time range as Barremian to Barremian, from 125.77 to 121.4 million years ago.
Scientists debate the average temperature of the region where Qantassaurus lived, with estimates ranging from -6 to over 5 degrees Celsius.
